title: Arabic grammar
about: From your very first sentence to everyday conversation, one short lesson at a time. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is Modern Standard Arabic, fully vowelled, with a reading in Latin letters.

units.title: Where, whose, and what you have
More than one: plurals and numbers

lessons.title: Reading the examples: the vowel marks
lessons.summary: How Arabic is written, and the small marks that show its vowels, so you can read every example in this course.

blocks.p: Arabic is written from right to left, and most letters join the letter after them. The letters mostly write **consonants**. The short vowels a, i and u are small marks above or below the letters.

blocks.means: a sound like a, i or u, made with the mouth open. The other sounds of speech, like b, k or s, are **consonants**.

blocks.p: Newspapers and street signs usually leave the vowel marks out: readers know the words. Every example in this course has them, because they show exactly how a word is said, and some of them, as you will see, are grammar.

**Long vowels** are written with letters: {{ا}} for ā, {{و}} for ū and {{ي}} for ī, as in {{بَابٌ|bābun}} “a door”, {{نُورٌ|nūrun}} “light” and {{كَبِيرٌ|kabīrun}} “big”. In the readings of this course, a line over a vowel (ā, ī, ū) means it is long: hold it about twice as long.

**Doubled marks at the end** of a word ({{ـٌ}}, {{ـً}}, {{ـٍ}}) add an n: {{كِتَابٌ|kitābun}}, {{كِتَابًا|kitāban}}, {{كِتَابٍ|kitābin}}. They mean “a”, as in “a book”. Which of the three a word has depends on its job in the sentence, which later lessons explain.

Two more signs: {{ء}} (hamza) is a short catch in the throat, like the break in the middle of “uh-oh”; it often sits on an alif, as in {{أَنَا|anā}} “I”. And {{ة}}, a round t, ends many words; you will meet it in the lesson on masculine and feminine. In the readings, ʾ is a hamza, ʿ is the letter {{ع}} (a sound made deep in the throat), and a dot under a letter (ḥ, ṣ, ḍ, ṭ, ẓ) marks a heavier sound than the plain one.

blocks.tip: The reading under each example is there to help you, not to replace the Arabic: read the Arabic first, then check. Tap an example to hear it.

mistakes.why: The n of -un is never written as a letter: the doubled mark ({{ـٌ}}) already says it.
“Big” has a long ī, written with {{ي}}: kabīrun. Short and long vowels make different words, so hold the long ones.

practice.q: Which mark is the vowel i?
practice.why: The kasra, a small line **below** the letter, is i.

practice.q: What does the doubled mark at the end of {{كِتَابٌ}} add?
practice.why: {{ـٌ}} is said -un, and it means “a”: kitābun, a book.

practice.q: Which word has a long ā?
practice.why: The {{ا}} after the first letter makes a long ā: bābun.

practice.q: Read this word aloud, then check: {{مُدَرِّسٌ}}
practice.why: The shadda on {{ر}} says it twice: mu-dar-ri-sun.

lessons.title: Nouns, and the word for “the”
lessons.summary: Say “a house” and “the house”: Arabic's word for “the”, and how it joins the word after it.

blocks.means: a word for a person, an animal, a place, a thing or an idea: teacher, cat, Cairo, book, love.

blocks.p: Arabic's word for “the” is {{الْـ|al-}}. It is written joined to the front of the noun: {{بَيْتٌ|baytun}} is “a house”, {{الْبَيْتُ|al-baytu}} is “the house”.

There is no separate word for “a”. A noun ending in a doubled mark (-un) already means “a”. With {{الْـ}}, the doubled mark goes, and a single mark is left: “the house” is {{الْبَيْتُ|al-baytu}}, never {{الْبَيْتٌ}}.

**Sun letters.** Before 14 of the letters, the l of {{الْـ}} isn't said: the next letter is doubled instead, and gets a shadda. The l is still written. So {{الشَّمْسُ}} “the sun” is said ash-shamsu, not al-shamsu. These letters are called sun letters, after {{شَمْسٌ|shamsun}} “sun”. The others are moon letters, after {{قَمَرٌ|qamarun}} “moon”: with them the l is said, {{الْقَمَرُ|al-qamaru}}.

table: Sun letters: the l is not said
Moon letters: the l is said
{{ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن}}
{{ء ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي}}

blocks.p: **After a vowel**, the a of {{الْـ}} isn't said either: “in the house” is {{فِي الْبَيْتِ|fī l-bayti}}. The readings in this course write it the way you hear it.

blocks.tip: Say every new noun once with {{الْـ}} and once without. Your ear will soon tell the sun letters from the moon letters by itself.

mistakes.why: A word with {{الْـ}} never has the doubled mark: that mark means “a”, and a word can't be “a” and “the” at once.
Before a sun letter the l is silent and has no mark of its own: say ash-shamsu.

practice.why: {{الْـ}} plus the noun, with a single mark at the end: al-kitābu.

practice.q: In which word is the l of {{الْـ}} **not** said?
practice.why: {{ش}} is a sun letter: ash-shamsu.
The doubled mark -un means “a”: waladun, a boy.
{{س}} is a sun letter, so the l is silent and the s is doubled.

lessons.title: Masculine and feminine
lessons.summary: Every Arabic noun is masculine or feminine. Learn the sign that marks most feminine words.

blocks.means: whether a word is **masculine** (like “he”) or **feminine** (like “she”). In Arabic every noun has one, even the words for things: a door is masculine, a car is feminine.

blocks.p: Most feminine nouns end in {{ة}}, a round t called tāʾ marbūṭa. At the end of a sentence it sounds -a; with an ending after it, -at-: {{سَيَّارَةٌ|sayyāratun}} “a car”.
Many words for people come in pairs: add {{ة}} to the masculine word and you have the feminine one.

A few common feminine nouns have no {{ة}}; learn them as you meet them: {{أُمٌّ|ummun}} “mother”, {{بِنْتٌ|bintun}} “girl, daughter”, {{شَمْسٌ|shamsun}} “sun”, {{أَرْضٌ|arḍun}} “earth, ground”, {{يَدٌ|yadun}} “hand”, {{عَيْنٌ|ʿaynun}} “eye”, {{حَرْبٌ|ḥarbun}} “war”, and the names of most countries and cities, like {{مِصْرُ|miṣru}} “Egypt”.

blocks.tip: Why it matters: words that describe a noun, and verbs, change to match its gender. The next lessons show how.

mistakes.why: A woman or a girl is a {{طَالِبَةٌ}}, with {{ة}}.

practice.why: {{مَدِينَةٌ}} ends in {{ة}}.
It has no {{ة}}, but a mother is a woman: it's one of the feminine words to learn by heart.
Add {{ة}} to the masculine word.

lessons.title: Roots: families of words
lessons.summary: Most Arabic words are built on three consonants that carry a meaning. Knowing them helps you guess new words.

blocks.means: the three consonants (sometimes four) that a family of Arabic words share and that carry its basic meaning. The vowels and extra letters around them make the different words.

blocks.p: The letters {{ك ت ب}} (k-t-b) carry the idea of writing. Put vowels and a few extra letters around them, always keeping them in the same order, and you get a whole family of words:

table: ā-i: the one who does it
ma-: the place where it's done
ma-…-ū: what it is done to

blocks.means: a shape of vowels and extra letters that is put around a root. The same pattern gives the same kind of meaning with every root: ā-i makes the one who does it, like {{كَاتِبٌ}} “writer”.

blocks.p: So the same shapes work with other roots. {{د ر س}} (d-r-s) is about studying: {{دَرَسَ|darasa}} “he studied”, {{دَرْسٌ|darsun}} “a lesson”, {{مَدْرَسَةٌ|madrasatun}} “a school”, {{مُدَرِّسٌ|mudarrisun}} “a teacher”. {{ع ل م}} (ʿ-l-m) is about knowing: {{عِلْمٌ|ʿilmun}} “knowledge, science”, {{عَالِمٌ|ʿālimun}} “a scientist”, {{مُعَلِّمٌ|muʿallimun}} “a teacher”.

blocks.tip: Many dictionaries list words by their root: to find {{مَكْتَبَةٌ}}, look under {{ك ت ب}}. When you meet a new word, look for three letters you already know.

mistakes.why: A root's letters always keep their order: k-t-b, so ma-k-t-a-b-a.

practice.q: Which word belongs to the same family as {{كِتَابٌ}}?
practice.why: {{كَاتِبٌ}} “writer” has the same root, {{ك ت ب}}.

practice.q: {{د ر س}} is about studying. What does {{مَدْرَسَةٌ}} probably mean?
options: a place for studying: a school
practice.why: ma-…-a is a pattern for places.
mu- is an extra part of the pattern; the root is ʿ-l-m, knowing.

practice.q: Put the root letters of {{كَاتِبٌ}} “writer” in order.

lessons.title: “This is…”: sentences without “is”
lessons.summary: Make your first sentences, like “This is a book” and “The house is big”, with no word for “is”.

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: The house is big.
the person or thing a sentence is about. In “The house is big”, the subject is “the house”.

blocks.p: In English, “is”, “am” and “are” link the subject to what you say about it. In the present, Arabic leaves them out: you just put the two side by side. {{الْبَيْتُ|al-baytu}} “the house” + {{كَبِيرٌ|kabīrun}} “big” gives {{الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ.|al-baytu kabīrun.}} “The house is big.”
The subject usually has {{الْـ}} “the”, and what you say about it usually doesn't. Both end in -u: one u on {{الْبَيْتُ}}, and -un on {{كَبِيرٌ}}.
“This is” works the same way: {{هَذَا|hādhā}} “this” for a masculine noun, {{هَذِهِ|hādhihi}} for a feminine one, then the noun: {{هَذَا كِتَابٌ.|hādhā kitābun.}} “This is a book.”

blocks.tip: What you say about a feminine subject is feminine too: {{الْغُرْفَةُ صَغِيرَةٌ}}, with {{ة}} on both words.

mistakes.why: {{سَيَّارَةٌ}} is feminine, so “this” is {{هَذِهِ}}.
With {{الْـ}} on both words it means “the big house”, a phrase, not a sentence. To say “the house is big”, leave {{الْـ}} off the second word.

practice.q: How do you say “The room is small”?
practice.why: Subject with {{الْـ}}, then what you say about it without {{الْـ}}, both feminine.

practice.q: Which word completes “This is a city”: ___ {{مَدِينَةٌ}}?
practice.why: {{مَدِينَةٌ}} ends in {{ة}}: it's feminine.

practice.q: How do you say “This is a book”?

lessons.title: I, you, he, she: pronouns
lessons.summary: The words for I, you, he, she, we and they, and Arabic's different words for “you”.

blocks.means: a short word that stands for a noun: I, you, she, they.

blocks.p: Arabic has a different “you” for a man, for a woman and for a group. And as you saw in the last lesson, “am”, “is” and “are” aren't said: {{أَنَا طَالِبٌ.|anā ṭālibun.}} is “I am a student.”

table: a man, or a masculine thing
a woman, or a feminine thing
any group with me in it
a group of men, or of men and women
a group of men, or of men and women

blocks.p: “It” is {{هُوَ}} or {{هِيَ}}, depending on the noun's gender: the book is “he”, the car is “she”.

There are also words for a group of women only ({{أَنْتُنَّ|antunna}} “you”, {{هُنَّ|hunna}} “they”) and for exactly two people ({{أَنْتُمَا|antumā}} “you two”, {{هُمَا|humā}} “they two”). You will hear them less; a later lesson comes back to the two.

blocks.tip: Once you learn verbs, you'll see that Arabic often leaves the pronoun out: the verb already shows who it is.

mistakes.tr: You are a student. (to a woman)
mistakes.why: Talking to a woman, “you” is {{أَنْتِ}}, anti, with i.
There is no word for “am”: put {{أَنَا}} and the noun side by side.

practice.q: You are talking to a woman. “You” is…
practice.why: {{أَنْتِ}}, anti, is for one woman.
{{هِيَ}}, hiya, is “she” (or “it” for a feminine thing).

practice.q: “The car? ___ is new.” Which word is “it”? {{السَّيَّارَةُ؟ ___ جَدِيدَةٌ.}}
practice.why: {{سَيَّارَةٌ}} is feminine, so “it” is {{هِيَ}}.

practice.q: How does a woman say “I am a doctor”?

lessons.title: Describing things: adjectives
lessons.summary: Say “a big house” and “the big house”: the adjective comes after the noun and matches it.

blocks.means: a word that describes a noun: big, new, happy.

blocks.p: In Arabic the adjective comes **after** the noun: {{بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ|baytun kabīrun}} “a big house”, word for word “house big”.
It matches the noun in three ways: in gender ({{ة}} for a feminine noun), in “a” or “the”, and in its ending. So “the big house” has {{الْـ}} twice: {{الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ|al-baytu l-kabīru}}.

Compare this with the last lessons. {{الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ}}, with “the” twice, is only a phrase: “the big house”. {{الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ}}, with “the” on the noun alone, is a sentence: “The house is big.” That one {{الْـ}} makes all the difference.

ex.tr: The old city is very beautiful.

blocks.p: Two adjectives? Add them one after the other, each matching the noun: {{سَيَّارَةٌ صَغِيرَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ|sayyāratun ṣaghīratun jadīdatun}} “a small new car”.

blocks.tip: Arabic also uses {{الْـ}} for things in general, where English uses no word: “coffee is delicious” is {{الْقَهْوَةُ لَذِيذَةٌ}}, “the coffee is delicious”.

mistakes.why: The adjective comes after the noun.
{{سَيَّارَةٌ}} is feminine, so the adjective takes {{ة}} too.

practice.why: “The” on both words, and {{ة}} on both.
{{الْـ}} on the noun only: it's a sentence.

practice.q: How do you say “a beautiful city”?

lessons.title: Asking questions
lessons.summary: Ask yes-or-no questions, and ask who, what, where, when, how, how many and why.

blocks.p: To turn a sentence into a yes-or-no question, put {{هَلْ|hal}} in front of it. Nothing else changes: {{أَنْتَ مَشْغُولٌ.|anta mashghūlun.}} “You are busy.” becomes {{هَلْ أَنْتَ مَشْغُولٌ؟|hal anta mashghūlun?}} “Are you busy?”
Arabic's question mark faces the other way: {{؟}}. In speech you can also just raise your voice at the end, without {{هَلْ}}. The answers are {{نَعَمْ|naʿam}} “yes” and {{لَا|lā}} “no”.

table: {{مَا اسْمُكَ؟|mā smuka?}} What is your name?
{{مَاذَا تُرِيدُ؟|mādhā turīdu?}} What do you want?
{{أَيْنَ الْفُنْدُقُ؟|ayna l-funduqu?}} Where is the hotel?
{{مَتَى الْحَفْلَةُ؟|matā l-ḥaflatu?}} When is the party?
{{كَمْ عُمْرُكَ؟|kam ʿumruka?}} How old are you?
{{بِكَمْ هَذَا؟|bikam hādhā?}} How much is this?
{{لِمَاذَا أَنْتَ هُنَا؟|limādhā anta hunā?}} Why are you here?

ex.note: before {{الْـ}}, {{هَلْ}} takes an i to join on: hali
to a woman: ḥāluki; to a man: ḥāluka

blocks.tip: The question word comes first and the rest stays as it was: {{أَيْنَ}} + {{الْفُنْدُقُ}} is “Where is the hotel?”

mistakes.why: {{هَلْ}} is only for yes-or-no questions; a question with a question word doesn't need it.
Before {{الْـ}}, {{هَلْ}} becomes {{هَلِ}}: hali l-maṭʿamu.

practice.why: {{أَيْنَ}}, ayna, is “where”. {{مَتَى}} is “when”, {{كَيْفَ}} “how”.

practice.q: How do you ask “Is the hotel near?”
practice.why: A yes-or-no question: {{هَلْ}} in front of the sentence.

lessons.title: This, that, these: pointing words
lessons.summary: Point at things near and far, and tell “this book” from “this is a book”.

blocks.p: You have met {{هَذَا}} and {{هَذِهِ}}. Here is the whole family:

blocks.tip: The long ā in {{هَذَا}} (hādhā), {{هَذِهِ}} (hādhihi) and {{ذَلِكَ}} (dhālika) isn't written as a letter, but it is said all the same.

blocks.p: **“This book” or “This is a book”?** A pointing word before a noun **with** {{الْـ}} makes a phrase: {{هَذَا الْكِتَابُ|hādhā l-kitābu}} “this book”. Before a noun **without** {{الْـ}}, it makes a sentence: {{هَذَا كِتَابٌ.|hādhā kitābun.}} “This is a book.”
To say “This is **the** book”, put {{هُوَ}} or {{هِيَ}} in the middle: {{هَذَا هُوَ الْكِتَابُ.|hādhā huwa l-kitābu.}}
For things (not people) in the plural, Arabic says {{هَذِهِ}} and {{تِلْكَ}}: {{هَذِهِ الْكُتُبُ|hādhihi l-kutubu}} “these books”. A later lesson explains why.

mistakes.why: To say “this book is new”, the book needs {{الْـ}}. Without it, the sentence means “This is a new book.”
{{رَجُلٌ}} “man” is masculine.

practice.why: Feminine, and a phrase: {{الْـ}} on the noun.
No {{الْـ}} on the noun: it's a sentence.

practice.q: How do you ask “What is this?”

lessons.title: In, on, from: little words for place and time
lessons.summary: Say where things are and where you're going, and meet the -i ending that follows these words.

blocks.means: a small word that links a noun to the rest of the sentence, often to say where or when: in, on, from, to, with.

blocks.p: Arabic's most common prepositions:

table: {{أَمَامَ الْفُنْدُقِ|amāma l-funduqi}} in front of the hotel

blocks.p: **The -i ending.** Look at the end of each noun: after a preposition it ends in -i. {{الْبَيْتُ|al-baytu}} becomes {{فِي الْبَيْتِ|fī l-bayti}}. Without “the”, -un becomes -in: {{صَدِيقٌ|ṣadīqun}}, but {{مَعَ صَدِيقٍ|maʿa ṣadīqin}}.

blocks.means: the vowel at the end of an Arabic noun, which changes with the noun's job in the sentence: -u, -a or -i (-un, -an or -in when it means “a”). After a preposition it is always -i.

blocks.p: Before {{الْـ}}, {{مِنْ}} becomes {{مِنَ|mina}} and {{عَنْ}} becomes {{عَنِ|ʿani}}, just as {{هَلْ}} became {{هَلِ}}: two consonants can't meet.

Three prepositions are so short that they are written joined to the next word: {{بِـ|bi-}} “with, by”, {{لِـ|li-}} “for, to” and {{كَـ|ka-}} “like”: {{بِالسَّيَّارَةِ|bi-s-sayyārati}} “by car”. With {{الْـ}}, {{لِـ}} drops the alif: {{لِلْبَيْتِ|lil-bayti}} “for the house”.

ex.tr: The book is on the table.
The road to the airport is long.
The restaurant is in front of the hotel.
This present is for the teacher.

blocks.p: Names of most countries and cities don't take -un or -in: after a preposition they end in -a. {{مِصْرُ|miṣru}} “Egypt”, {{أَنَا مِنْ مِصْرَ.|anā min miṣra.}} “I'm from Egypt.”

blocks.tip: Sentences like {{الْكِتَابُ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ}} need no “is” either: “the book, on the table” already says “The book is on the table.”

mistakes.why: After a preposition, the noun ends in -i.
Before {{الْـ}}, {{مِنْ}} becomes {{مِنَ}}: mina l-madrasati.
{{لِـ}} with {{الْـ}} is written {{لِلْـ}}: the alif drops.

practice.why: After {{فِي}}, the noun ends in -i.
{{إِلَى}}, ilā, is “to”; {{مِنْ}} is “from”, {{عَلَى}} “on”.
Without “the”, -un becomes -in after a preposition.

practice.tr: The book is on the table.

practice.q: How do you say “I'm from Egypt”?
practice.why: Country names end in -a after a preposition: {{مِصْرَ}}.

lessons.title: My, your, his: endings on nouns
lessons.summary: Say “my book”, “your house”, “her name”: Arabic adds a short ending to the noun.

blocks.p: Arabic has no separate words for “my”, “your”, “his” and so on. A short ending is joined to the noun instead. The noun then drops {{الْـ}} and its doubled mark: the ending already says whose it is.

blocks.means: a short ending joined to a noun to say whose it is, like “my” or “your” in English: {{كِتَابِي}} “my book”.

blocks.p: **The round t opens up.** A word ending in {{ة}} writes it as an ordinary {{ت}} before an ending, and the t is said: {{سَيَّارَةٌ|sayyāratun}} “a car”, {{سَيَّارَتِي|sayyāratī}} “my car”, {{سَيَّارَتُهَا|sayyāratuhā}} “her car”.

The case ending stays between the noun and the ending: {{بَيْتُهُ|baytuhu}} “his house”, but {{فِي بَيْتِهِ|fī baytihi}} “in his house” (-i after {{فِي}}; and -hu becomes -hi after an i). Only “my” swallows the case ending: {{بَيْتِي|baytī}}, wherever it stands.

A noun with an ending counts as “the”, so an adjective after it takes {{الْـ}}: {{سَيَّارَتِي الْجَدِيدَةُ|sayyāratī l-jadīdatu}} “my new car”. And without {{الْـ}}, it is a sentence: {{سَيَّارَتِي جَدِيدَةٌ.|sayyāratī jadīdatun.}} “My car is new.”

ex.note: to a man; to a woman: {{مَا اسْمُكِ؟|mā smuki?}}

blocks.tip: {{اسْمٌ}} “name” starts with a vowel that is only said at the start of a sentence: {{اسْمِي سَارَةُ|ismī sāratu}}, but {{مَا اسْمُكَ؟|mā smuka?}}.

mistakes.why: A noun with an ending never has {{الْـ}} too.
{{ة}} becomes {{ت}} before an ending.

practice.why: The ending -ī, and no {{الْـ}}.
-hā is “her”.
{{ة}} becomes {{ت}}, then -unā.

lessons.title: “I have”: at me, for me, with me
lessons.summary: Arabic has no verb “to have”: it says “at me”, “for me” or “with me”.

blocks.p: To say “I have”, Arabic says “at me (there is)…”: {{عِنْدِي|ʿindī}}, made of {{عِنْدَ}} “at” and the ending “my”, then what you have: {{عِنْدِي سَيَّارَةٌ.|ʿindī sayyāratun.}} “I have a car.” The thing you have keeps -un: in Arabic it is the subject of the sentence.

Two other little words do the same job. {{لِـ}} “for” is used for family and for things that last: {{لِي أَخٌ.|lī akhun.}} “I have a brother.” With the other endings it becomes {{لَـ}}: {{لَكَ}}, {{لَهُ}}, {{لَهَا}}, {{لَنَا}}. And {{مَعَ}} “with” means you have it on you, now: {{مَعِي مَالٌ.|maʿī mālun.}} “I have money on me.”

**Asking:** {{هَلْ عِنْدَكَ قَلَمٌ؟|hal ʿindaka qalamun?}} “Do you have a pen?” **Not having:** put {{لَيْسَ|laysa}} in front: {{لَيْسَ عِنْدِي وَقْتٌ.|laysa ʿindī waqtun.}} “I don't have time.” (A later lesson explains {{لَيْسَ}}.)

The same endings go on every preposition: {{مِنْهُ|minhu}} “from him”, {{مَعَهَا|maʿahā}} “with her”, {{إِلَيْكَ|ilayka}} “to you”, {{عَنْهُمْ|ʿanhum}} “about them”. After i, ī or ay, -hu becomes -hi: {{فِيهِ|fīhi}} “in it”, {{عَلَيْهِ|ʿalayhi}} “on it”.

ex.tr: He has a son and a daughter.
Have you got a pen on you?
ex.note: to a man; a question just by the voice

blocks.tip: {{عِنْدِي}} is the everyday word: when in doubt, use it.

mistakes.why: The thing you have is the subject, so it keeps -un (in English it would be an object, but not in Arabic).
With an ending, {{لِـ}} becomes {{لَـ}}: lahu. Only “my” is {{لِي}}.

practice.why: -hā is “her”, and the car keeps -un.
{{لَيْسَ}} makes it negative.

practice.q: Which fits best for “I've got money on me (right now)”?
practice.why: {{مَعَ}} “with” is for what you have on you.

practice.q: Ask a man: “Do you have a pen?”

lessons.title: “There is” and “there are”
lessons.summary: Say what there is in a place: “There's a café near the hotel.”

blocks.p: To say that something is in a place, start with the place, then the thing, without “the”: {{فِي الْغُرْفَةِ سَرِيرٌ.|fī l-ghurfati sarīrun.}} “There's a bed in the room.” (word for word: in the room, a bed).
Why the place first? An Arabic sentence doesn't start with a noun that means “a…” ({{سَرِيرٌ}}), so the place comes to the front.

You can also start with {{هُنَاكَ|hunāka}} “there”: {{هُنَاكَ مُشْكِلَةٌ.|hunāka mushkilatun.}} “There's a problem.” Written Arabic often uses {{يُوجَدُ|yūjadu}} “there is” (word for word: is found): {{يُوجَدُ مَطْعَمٌ قَرِيبٌ.|yūjadu maṭʿamun qarībun.}} “There's a restaurant nearby.”
**There isn't:** {{لَا يُوجَدُ|lā yūjadu}} or {{لَيْسَ هُنَاكَ|laysa hunāka}}: {{لَا يُوجَدُ وَقْتٌ.|lā yūjadu waqtun.}} “There's no time.” **Is there…?:** {{هَلْ هُنَاكَ…؟}} or {{هَلْ يُوجَدُ…؟}}

ex.tr: There's a café near the hotel.
There's a book on the table.

blocks.tip: Compare {{الْكِتَابُ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ.}} “The book is on the table.” (a book you both know) with {{عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ كِتَابٌ.}} “There's a book on the table.” (some book).

mistakes.tr: There's a book on the table.
mistakes.why: A sentence doesn't start with a noun meaning “a…”: put the place first.
“There is” brings in something new: no {{الْـ}}.

practice.q: “There's a café near the hotel” is…
practice.why: Start with {{هُنَاكَ}}, and the café without “the”.
{{لَا يُوجَدُ}} is “there isn't”.

lessons.title: “The teacher's book”: two nouns together
lessons.summary: Put two nouns side by side to say whose something is, or what kind it is: “the door of the house”, “a cup of coffee”.

blocks.p: To say “the teacher's book” or “the door of the house”, Arabic puts the two nouns side by side: first the thing, then whose it is. {{كِتَابُ الْمُعَلِّمِ|kitābu l-muʿallimi}} “the teacher's book”, word for word “book the-teacher”.

blocks.means: two (or more) nouns side by side, the second saying whose the first is or what kind it is: {{بَابُ الْبَيْتِ}} “the door of the house”. The word means “adding”.

blocks.p: **Three rules.** 1) The first noun never has {{الْـ}} or the doubled mark, even though it means “the”: {{بَابُ|bābu}}, not {{الْبَابُ}} or {{بَابٌ}}. 2) The second noun ends in -i (or -in), as after a preposition: {{الْبَيْتِ|al-bayti}}. 3) A {{ة}} on the first noun is said with its t: {{سَيَّارَةُ أَبِي|sayyāratu abī}} “my father's car”.

If the second noun has “the” (or an ending like “my”), the pair means “the…”: {{بَابُ الْبَيْتِ}} “the door of the house”. If not, it means “a…”: {{فِنْجَانُ قَهْوَةٍ|finjānu qahwatin}} “a cup of coffee”. The pair also says what kind: {{مَدْرَسَةُ اللُّغَاتِ|madrasatu l-lughāti}} “the language school”.
An adjective comes after the whole pair, matching the noun it describes: {{سَيَّارَةُ أَبِي الْجَدِيدَةُ|sayyāratu abī l-jadīdatu}} “my father's new car”.

ex.tr: The door of the house is open.

blocks.tip: Chains work too: {{بَابُ بَيْتِ الْمُدِيرِ|bābu bayti l-mudīri}} “the door of the manager's house”. Only the last noun can have {{الْـ}}.

mistakes.why: The first noun never takes {{الْـ}} (or the doubled mark).
The second noun ends in -i.

practice.why: First noun bare, second with {{الْـ}} and -i.
The second noun has no “the”, so the pair means “a…”.
The adjective comes after the whole pair.

practice.q: How do you say “the teacher's book”?

lessons.title: “Is not”: لَيْسَ
lessons.summary: Say “I'm not tired”, “The shop isn't open”: Arabic's “is not” changes with the person.

blocks.p: Sentences without a verb (“The house is big”) are made negative with {{لَيْسَ|laysa}} “is not”. Unlike “is”, which isn't said, “is not” is a real word, and it changes with the person:

**The -a ending.** What you say about the subject now ends in -a, or -an without “the”: {{أَنَا مُتْعَبٌ.|anā mutʿabun.}} “I'm tired.” becomes {{لَسْتُ مُتْعَبًا.|lastu mutʿaban.}} “I'm not tired.” The -an is written with an extra alif: {{ـًا}}.
{{لَيْسَ}} can come after the subject or before it: {{الْمَحَلُّ لَيْسَ مَفْتُوحًا.|al-maḥallu laysa maftūḥan.}} or {{لَيْسَ الْمَحَلُّ مَفْتُوحًا.}} “The shop isn't open.”

ex.note: a man speaking; a woman says {{لَسْتُ مُتْعَبَةً|lastu mutʿabatan}}

blocks.tip: Only a noun or an adjective after {{لَيْسَ}} takes -a. A place doesn't change: {{هِيَ لَيْسَتْ فِي الْبَيْتِ.}} “She isn't at home.” And with {{عِنْدِي}} the thing keeps -un: {{لَيْسَ عِنْدِي فِكْرَةٌ.}}

mistakes.why: {{لَا}} is for verbs; a sentence without a verb takes {{لَيْسَ}}.
After {{لَيْسَ}}, the adjective ends in -an.

practice.why: {{لَسْتُ}} for “I am not”, and -an on the adjective.
{{لَيْسَتْ}} for “she”, and -an.

practice.q: How do you say “We're not from here”?
